units.translation: Of the aorist ἐπίθησα, whose participle πιθήσας [having obeyed] is used frequently in epic poetry for πεισθείς [having been persuaded] or πεποιθώς [having trusted], one example is found in Aeschylus.
Thus Abreschius for πειθήσασα [having persuaded].
Πλούρα [more] are examples of the second aorist ἔπιθον [I persuaded].
πείθων [persuading] first in M.

Examples of the imperatives πείθου [be persuaded] and πείθεσθε [be persuaded] wrongly introduced for the aorist πιθοῦ [obey] and πιθέσθαι [to obey] will be given below. The imperative of the perfect πέπεισμαι [I have been persuaded] is πέπεισθι [be persuaded].

where in M is written ζτ. (i.e. Ζήτει [seek]), because this form had offended the scribe, of which no other examples are found. πέπισθι or πέποισθι [be persuaded] Veitch wished to be written, Greek verbs irregular p. 458, third edition, and after Veitch Gilbert in Ritschl's Acta Soc. philol. vol. 2 p. 330. The participle is
Future middle
which according to the sense of each passage can be rendered in Latin by the words persuasum habeo [I have persuaded myself], obsequor [I comply], credo [I believe], confido [I trust].

in the manuscripts of the tragedians not rarely written with a diphthong even without regard to the meter, as in the anapaestic verse Sept. 1065 εἶσιν. τίς ἂν οὖν τὰ πίθοιτο? [he will go. Who then would obey these things?]; where πείθοιτο [would obey] M, but some copies πίθοιτο [would obey]. Eum. 794 ἐμοὶ πίθεσθε μὴ βαρυστόνως φέρειν [obey me, not to bear heavily], where Turnebus corrected what is in M πείθεσθε [obey]. Ag. 206 βαρεῖα μὲν κὴρ τὸ μὴ πιθέσθαι [heavy is the doom of not obeying]. Thus here too Turnebus: in M πειθέσθαι [to obey], the accent itself showing the aorist πιθέσθαι [to obey], not the present πείθεσθαι [to be persuaded]. Correctly indeed ib. 943 at the beginning of the trimeter (in the part of the play lost from M) πιθοῦ [obey] in the copies. In M perhaps here too πείθου [be persuaded] was written, as in all other places, whose meter either allows or demands πιθοῦ [obey], but never demands πείθου [be persuaded], by which indication recent editors have everywhere restored the simple vowel.
simple
where correctly some copies πιθοῦ [obey].
Thus in both places Blomfield for πείθου [be persuaded].
thus Stanley for πείθου [be persuaded]

Blomfield for πείθεσθέ μοι πείθεσθε [obey me, obey]. The same inconsistency of the codex is in Sophocles, about which I have spoken in Lex. Soph. p. 394. The authority of the books in this matter is absolutely nothing, since also λειπεῖν [to leave] and λειπών [having left] are found written in ancient manuscripts not rarely for λιπεῖν [to leave] and λιπών [having left].
For in no way will you persuade him.
Say something else and comfort me with whatever you can persuade me.
The heavenly dust persuades me.
I persuade him with a word.
I was persuading no one of anything.
And if I do not persuade you of something similar to these things.
For indeed I persuaded you to kill your mother's body.
You persuaded the Fates to make mortals immortal.
I will persuade the public.
He was persuading with such a speech about us.
Having been persuaded by gifts to Minos.
If a pious word could persuade.
I was not able to persuade the Titans.
You led Hesione, having persuaded her to be your wedded wife.
You might persuade, if you persuade; but perhaps you would fail to persuade.
Be persuaded by the dead, having killed your mother.
Persuaded by your laments.
Persuaded by empty hopes.
By whom were you persuaded, and by whose counsels?
